entities.summary:
Rice University in Houston, Texas, founded in 1912 through a bequest by William Marsh Rice (a Houston businessman murdered in 1900 by his valet and attorney in a poisoning scheme — his murder case is one of American history's most sensational), is consistently ranked among America's top 20 universities despite enrolling only 4,000 undergraduates — the smallest enrollment of any top-20 research university. Rice's engineering and architecture schools, its proximity to NASA's Johnson Space Center, and its free tuition (1912-1964) made it the 'Harvard of the South' in STEM education.

William Marsh Rice's 1891 will left his entire fortune (approximately $4.6 million, roughly $150 million today) to found a free educational institution in Houston. His 1900 murder by Patrick Morris (valet) and Albert Patrick (attorney), who forged a new will leaving the estate to Patrick, was foiled when Rice's secretary alerted police; the subsequent trial was sensational. Rice University opened tuition-free in 1912, attracting top Texas students who couldn't afford Ivy League tuition.

Rice's space connection: the university sits 8 km from NASA's Johnson Space Center; Rice's President Kenneth Pitzer hosted John F. Kennedy's 1962 'We Choose to Go to the Moon' speech in Rice Stadium (80,000 capacity), which announced the Apollo program to a national audience. Rice's engineering and computational science programs are disproportionately elite given the university's size — producing Nobel laureates and NASA astronauts.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Rice University — founded by murder victim's bequest, opened tuition-free, adjacent to NASA, and the site of Kennedy's Moon speech — punches far above its 4,000-student enrollment in STEM research prestige and American cultural symbolism.
